table.caption: Five combinations of wheat and tractors Dornia (an invented country) can produce in a year using all its resources efficiently (invented data for practice)

opportunity-cost-ppc-s2.title: Bellmark's production possibilities, then and now

items.q: Label this production possibilities curve for an economy that makes pizzas (on the horizontal axis) and robots (on the vertical axis).

why.correct: Each axis is one of the two goods, by name: Pizzas across, Robots up. The curve is the PPC.

items.q: A recession leaves many factories idle and many workers without jobs. Place point U to show what the economy produces.

why.correct: Idle resources mean the economy produces less of both goods than it could: a point inside the PPC.

items.q: Place point Z at a combination of pizzas and robots the economy cannot produce with its current resources and technology.

why.correct: Combinations outside the PPC are unattainable now; they need more resources or better technology.

items.q: Every worker and machine is employed in its best use. Place point F to show one combination the economy could produce.

why.correct: Using all resources efficiently puts the economy on the PPC.

items.q: A new technology raises how much of both goods the economy can make. Show the change on the graph.

why.correct: Better technology lets the economy make more of both goods: the whole PPC shifts outward.

key.because: a new technology that raises output of both goods

items.q: A hurricane destroys many factories and farms. Show the change on the graph.

why.correct: Fewer resources mean less of both goods can be made: the PPC shifts inward.

key.because: a hurricane that destroys factories and farms

items.q: Using the table, what is the opportunity cost per million bushels of wheat when Dornia moves from combination 2 to combination 3?

why.correct: Dornia gains 10 million bushels of wheat and gives up $18 - 14 = 4$ thousand tractors, so each million bushels costs $\frac{4}{10} = 0.4$ thousand tractors.

mistakes.why: You divided the wheat gained by the tractors given up. Opportunity cost is what is given up per unit gained: 4 / 10.
That is the total cost of the 10 million bushels. The question asks per million bushels: divide by 10.

items.q: Using the table, how many thousand tractors does Dornia give up in total to move from combination 3 to combination 4?

why.correct: Tractors fall from 14 thousand to 8 thousand: $14 - 8 = 6$ thousand tractors given up for 10 million more bushels of wheat.

mistakes.why: That is the number of tractors still made at combination 4. The cost is how many were given up: 14 - 8.
That is the wheat gained. The opportunity cost is measured in the good given up, tractors.

items.q: What does the table show about Dornia's opportunity cost of wheat as it makes more wheat?
options: It stays the same: each extra 10 million bushels costs 2 thousand tractors
It rises: each extra 10 million bushels costs more tractors than the last
It falls: wheat gets cheaper to make as Dornia makes more
It is impossible to find from a table

why.correct: The tractors given up for each extra 10 million bushels are 2, 4, 6 and 8 thousand: increasing opportunity cost, so the PPC is bowed out.
options: Only the first step costs 2 thousand; later steps cost more.
Right: 2, then 4, then 6, then 8 thousand tractors.
The cost of wheat rises, not falls, as Dornia moves along.
The differences between rows give the costs directly.

items.q: Could Dornia produce 25 million bushels of wheat and 14 thousand tractors in the same year?
options: No: that combination lies outside its PPC
Yes: it lies inside its PPC, with resources to spare
Yes: it lies on its PPC
Yes, once it gives up some wheat

why.correct: At 20 million bushels Dornia can make at most 14 thousand tractors; making more wheat means fewer tractors, so 25 million and 14 thousand is outside the curve.
options: Right: more wheat than combination 3 with the same tractors is out of reach.
A point inside would need fewer tractors than the curve allows at 25 million bushels.
Points on the curve between combinations 3 and 4 have fewer than 14 thousand tractors.
Giving up wheat would bring the point back toward the curve, but the question asks about 25 million bushels.

items.q: Dornia is producing 20 million bushels of wheat and 10 thousand tractors. What does this tell you?
options: It is producing at an efficient point
It has the best technology in the world
It has just lost a large share of its factories in a hurricane
Some of its resources are unemployed or used inefficiently

why.correct: With 20 million bushels Dornia could make 14 thousand tractors; making only 10 thousand puts it inside the PPC.
options: An efficient point lies on the curve: 14 thousand tractors at this wheat output.
The table says nothing about other countries' technology.
Being inside the curve shows idle resources; it does not say why.
Right: inside the curve, so resources are idle or misused.

items.q: What change could explain the move from the faded curve to the new one in the graph?
options: Bellmark puts its idle factories back to work
The price of machines rises
Bellmark gains more workers and better machines
Bellmark shifts workers from making food to making machines

why.correct: The whole curve moved outward, so Bellmark can now make more of both goods: more resources or better technology.
options: Using idle resources moves a point toward the existing curve; the curve itself stays put.
A price change does not change what can be produced.
Right: more or better resources shift the PPC out.
Moving workers between goods is a movement along the curve.

items.q: A combination of food and machines lay just outside Bellmark's faded curve. Where does it lie now?
options: It is still unattainable, because the whole curve shifted
It may now be attainable, on or inside the new curve
It is now inside the faded curve
It has moved to the horizontal axis

why.correct: An outward shift brings combinations that were just out of reach onto or inside the new curve.
options: The outward shift is exactly what makes some of those points reachable.
Right: the new curve reaches farther out.
The faded curve did not move; the point stays where it was relative to it.
A point does not move when the curve shifts.

items.q: Bellmark's new curve still bows outward. What does that shape tell you?
options: Resources are not equally good at making food and machines
Each extra unit of food costs the same number of machines
Bellmark has idle resources
Bellmark is unable to make more of both goods

why.correct: A bowed-out PPC shows increasing opportunity cost, because resources suited to one good are moved into the other as output of it grows.
options: Right: specialized resources give increasing opportunity cost.
A constant cost would give a straight line.
Idle resources put a point inside the curve; the shape says nothing about it.
The curve just shifted out, so it can make more of both than before.

items.q: Jordan's Saturday options, in order of preference, are a hike with friends, a paid work shift worth \$80, and studying. If Jordan goes on the hike, what is the opportunity cost?
options: The work shift and the studying, added together
Nothing, because the hike is free
The studying, because it ranks last
The \$80 work shift, the next-best choice

why.correct: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up, here the work shift. Jordan could not have done both other options with the same time.
options: Jordan could have done only one of the other two, so only the best of them counts.
Even a free activity costs the time that could have earned \$80.
The lowest-ranked option is not what Jordan would have done instead.
Right: only the next-best option counts.

items.q: A country's PPC is a straight line from 60 thousand shirts (and no jackets) to 20 thousand jackets (and no shirts). What is the opportunity cost of one jacket, in shirts?

why.correct: Making all 20 thousand jackets means giving up all 60 thousand shirts, so one jacket costs $\frac{60}{20} = 3$ shirts. A straight line means the cost is the same everywhere on it.

mistakes.why: That is the cost of one shirt in jackets (20 / 60). For a jacket, divide the shirts given up by the jackets gained: 60 / 20.

items.q: An economy spends more of its resources this year on factories and machines and less on consumer goods. What happens to its PPC in the future?
options: It shifts in, because people have fewer consumer goods today
It stays where it is, because total resources are unchanged
It shifts out farther, because the extra capital raises future production
It becomes a straight line

why.correct: Capital goods made today add to the resources of tomorrow, so the future PPC shifts out more than it would have.
options: Choosing capital goods over consumer goods is a movement along today's curve, not a loss of resources.
The new capital adds to future resources.
Right: more capital today means more production possible later.
The shape depends on how suited resources are to each good, not on this choice.

items.q: Why is a production possibilities curve usually bowed outward rather than straight?
options: Each resource is equally good at making both goods
Some resources are better at making one good than the other
The economy has idle resources at each point
Prices rise as output rises

why.correct: As an economy makes more of one good, it must use resources less and less suited to it, so each extra unit costs more of the other good.
options: Equally suited resources would give a straight line.
Right: specialized resources create increasing opportunity cost.
Idle resources put the economy inside the curve; they do not shape it.
The PPC shows quantities that can be produced, not prices.
